code.title: Tool calling: the model proposes, the app validates and runs
code.python:
# Tool calling end to end: the model only proposes calls; our code runs them.
TOOLS = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b}   # registry of real functions

print("user: what is 2+3?")
# Stand-in for the model: it returns structured calls, it executes nothing.
proposed = [("c1", "add", 2, 3), ("c2", "mul", 2, 3)]
results = {}
for call_id, name, a, b in proposed:
    print("model -> tool_use %s %s(%d, %d)" % (call_id, name, a, b))
    if name not in TOOLS:                  # the app validates before running
        results[call_id] = "error: unknown tool " + name
    else:
        results[call_id] = str(TOOLS[name](a, b))
    # each result is tied to the call id and goes back to the model
    print("app   -> tool_result %s %s" % (call_id, results[call_id]))
print("model -> final: 2 + 3 = " + results["c1"])

followUps: Most failures are in the arguments and in the loop around the model, not in the tool itself. The model can invent a tool name or a field, send a wrong type, or pass an id that belongs to another user, so validate against the schema and then check existence and ownership. Return tool errors as a result the model can read instead of throwing. A huge output can flood the context, so truncate it. A write tool retried after a timeout can run twice, so use an idempotency key. Results can also contain injected instructions, so treat them as data.

The model returns several tool_use blocks in one reply when the calls do not depend on each other, and your code may run them at the same time. Each block has its own id. You send back one tool_result per id (ids matter, order does not), all in the next message. Example: weather for 3 cities gives 3 calls; run together you wait about 1 second instead of 3. Do not parallelise calls where one needs another's output or both touch the same record. Cap concurrency, and turn one failure into an error result for that id only.

code.title: ReAct loop with a hard step budget
code.python:
# ReAct loop: action -> observation, repeated, with a hard step budget.
DOCS = {"faq": "see price list", "price list": "plan costs 42 dollars"}

def search(q):                       # the tool: returns an observation
    return DOCS.get(q, "no result")

def run(budget):
    print("== budget", budget, "==")
    queries = ["pricing", "faq", "price list"]   # scripted model actions
    for step in range(budget):                   # the step cap lives in code
        obs = search(queries[step])
        print("step %d: search(%s) -> %s" % (step + 1, queries[step], obs))
        if "42" in obs:                          # the model sees the answer
            print("finish:", obs)
            return
    print("stopped: budget of %d steps used" % budget)

run(5)
run(2)

followUps: Put the limits in code, not in the prompt. Use a hard step cap (for example 10), a token or cost cap, and a repeat check that stops when the same action with the same arguments appears 3 times or when observations bring nothing new. When a guard fires, return the partial work and say why it stopped. Also tell the model it may say it cannot finish, so giving up is an allowed action. The program above shows a budget stopping the loop at step 2.

Cost grows roughly with the square of the number of steps, because every step resends the whole transcript. If each step adds 1,000 tokens, step 1 reads 1,000, step 10 reads 10,000, and the total over 10 steps is about 55,000 input tokens, not 10,000. Reduce it by truncating big observations, summarising old steps, caching the stable prefix (system prompt and tool definitions), and capping steps. Latency grows the same way since each step is a full model call.

Test it with real model calls, not by reading it. Build 20 to 50 short user requests, including near-miss ones where the tool should not be used, and run them. Record which tool was chosen and whether the arguments were valid, and compare with the expected choice. Change one phrase of the description at a time and re-run several times, since output varies. Confusion between two similar tools is usually fixed by adding a line such as use this when X, not when Y.

There is no fixed number, but tool-choice accuracy drops and token cost rises as the list grows. Roughly, under 10 to 15 well-separated tools works well, and beyond about 20 mistakes become common. If each definition costs 100 to 300 tokens on every request, 40 tools add around 8,000 tokens per call. Fix it by merging overlapping tools, giving sub-agents their own small toolsets, or retrieving only the 5 to 8 relevant tools per request.

A replan should be triggered by evidence that the plan no longer fits, not by every hiccup. Typical triggers: a step fails after its retries, an observation contradicts an assumption the plan made, a needed resource is missing, or a step goes over its budget. Keep the finished steps, ask the planner to rewrite only the remaining ones using the new facts, and cap replans (for example 2) so it cannot churn forever. After the cap, stop and escalate to a human.

Use a small structured list, not free text. Each step has an id, a goal, the tool or worker, the ids it depends on, a status (pending, running, done, failed) and a reference to its result. Example: s1 search, s2 fetch (depends on s1), s3 summarise (depends on s2). Dependencies let you run independent steps in parallel and show a person the plan before approval. Store it as JSON, validate it against a schema, and save status after every step so a crash can resume.

Make deletion possible by design: every stored item carries the user id and a source reference. On a request, delete by user id from the profile table, the vector store, the summaries and the logs, and let backups expire on their schedule, then confirm. Summaries are the hard part because one summary can mix facts from many turns, so regenerate it from what remains or keep summaries per user only. Search for the id afterwards to prove nothing is left, and log the deletion itself without the content.

Keep exact facts out of the summary. Store ids, amounts, dates and decisions in structured profile fields, and keep the raw turns in an archive so details can be fetched again. Give the summariser a checklist of what must survive. Give the agent a recall tool so it can search the archive when the user mentions something not in the summary. Test it: plant an order number at turn 3, run to turn 60, and check the agent can still answer. Avoid summaries of summaries only.

Use a tool when the model decides to perform an action, and a resource when the application wants to hand over data to read. Tools are model-controlled and can have side effects, such as create_ticket. Resources are application-controlled and read-only, such as a file or a schema, identified by a URI and attached to the context by the app or the user. Example: a database server exposes the schema as a resource and run_query as a tool. If it needs approval or changes something, make it a tool.

Treat each server as a dependency and load only what a task needs. Enable servers per project or per agent, not globally. Allow-list tool names and hide the rest. With many tools, add a retrieval step that picks the 5 to 8 relevant ones from their descriptions for each request. Namespace tools by server to avoid name clashes, such as github.create_issue. Review servers, pin their versions and watch for description changes. Fewer, sharper tools improve choice accuracy and cut tokens.

A worker should return a short structured report, not its whole transcript. Include the status (done, failed, partial), the result, the evidence with source references, what it did not check, and any open question. Keep it to a few hundred tokens in a fixed schema so the orchestrator can merge reports in code. Example: status done, finding plan costs 42, source doc 7, confidence high. The full trace is stored separately for debugging. This keeps the orchestrator's context small and makes errors visible.

Give each worker its own area so they never write the same thing. Split work by disjoint files, records or sources, and let only one owner write each. For shared state, make workers return proposed changes and let the orchestrator apply them one at a time, or use locks or version checks (compare-and-set) so the second writer must retry. Example: two workers edit one file with version 7; the second finds the version is now 8 and re-reads. Read-only research workers cannot conflict, so prefer them.

code.title: Near-duplicate call guard

followUps: Normalise each call, then count how often the same normalised key appears. Lower-case the text, drop filler words, sort the remaining words and join them, so the Pricing and pricing match. Keep a counter per key and stop when one reaches a limit, such as 3. For fuzzier matching, compare word sets with Jaccard similarity (overlap divided by union) and treat 0.8 or more as a repeat. Cost is O(words) per call and O(calls) memory. The program above shows the idea.

Return a clear, honest partial result and mark the run as stopped by a guard. Include what was completed, which guard fired (for example the step cap of 10 or a repeated search), the evidence collected so far, and a suggested next step. Do not let the model pretend the task finished. Show the user a short message and, for important tasks, hand the trace to a human. Log the reason as a field so you can count how often each guard fires and turn those runs into tests.

LLM judges have known biases. They prefer longer answers, prefer the first option shown (position bias), favour text written by their own model family, and can be swayed by a confident tone. They also vary from run to run. Reduce this by swapping the order and averaging, scoring against a clear rubric with examples, using a different model family as judge, and comparing judge scores with 50 to 100 human labels to measure agreement. Use code checks for anything that can be checked exactly.

Big enough to detect the change you care about, and no bigger than you can maintain. Start with 50 to 100 tasks covering common, edge and adversarial cases, which finds large problems. With 100 tasks the 95 percent interval on a 70 percent success rate is about plus or minus 9 points, so proving a 5-point gain needs a few hundred runs. Repeat each task several times because agents are random, and grow the set from every production failure.

Make the agent stop in code and save its state outside the model. Write the transcript, the pending action, its arguments and the plan position to a database with a run id and status waiting_approval, then free the worker. When the person approves, an event loads the run, checks that the pending action is unchanged, executes it once using its idempotency key, and continues the loop. Add an expiry so abandoned approvals time out. This design also survives crashes and deploys.

Do not let the agent's own text be the only evidence. Build the approval card by code from the raw arguments (recipient, amount, file list), not from a model-written summary, so the explanation cannot hide a change. Show a diff against the user's original request, highlight unusual values, and require a second person for high amounts. Log everything. Test with red-team cases where the explanation is misleading, and treat any mismatch between summary and arguments as a block.

Compare using repeated runs, because agents give different results each time. Run the same suite 5 to 10 times per version and compare the average success and its spread. If 100 tasks give 70 percent before and 74 percent after, a gap of 4 points is within roughly plus or minus 9 points of noise, so it proves nothing. Use a paired comparison on the same tasks, a bootstrap confidence interval, and look at which tasks flipped. Count a change as real only when the interval excludes zero or the gain repeats.

Choose a better model when failures remain after the scaffolding is clean: tool descriptions are clear, arguments are validated, and traces show the model still reasons wrongly, such as missing a multi-step dependency. A quick test is to run the failing cases on a stronger model with nothing else changed; if success jumps, capability is the limit. Weigh the gain against cost and latency, and consider routing only the hard cases to the bigger model. If failures are loops or bad inputs, fix the code instead.

For a small system, a database plus a queue is enough and is easier to understand: one table for run state, one for the tool-call ledger, and a queue to wake runs. Choose a workflow engine when you have many long waits (days), timers, retries and branching, because it gives durable execution, replay and visibility out of the box. The cost is another system to run and rules such as keeping workflow code deterministic. I would start with the database and move to an engine when the state-machine code becomes the main work.

Store the schema version with the run and keep old versions available until runs using them finish. On resume, either use the old schema so the pending call still matches, or validate the saved arguments against the new schema. If they still fit, continue. If not, convert them with a small migration function, or park the run and ask for a human or a replan. Never send saved arguments to a tool that now expects different fields. Test it by upgrading a tool while a run is waiting.

Caching lowers the cost and delay of resending the same prefix, but it does not remove the real problem. The system prompt, tool definitions and earlier steps are identical each step, so a cache can read them at a fraction of the normal input price. Keep that prefix stable and put changing content at the end. A 40k-token page still fills the context and can push the model off track, so truncate it as well. Caching saves money; it does not stop the loop.

Compare what each observation adds to what the agent already has. Keep a set of seen result ids, urls or content hashes; if a new result has no unseen items, count it as no progress. After 2 or 3 such steps in a row, stop or change strategy. Example: a search returns the same 5 urls as before, so new items = 0. For free text, compare the overlap of word sets; above 0.8 means mostly repeated. Cost is O(size of result) per step with a set kept in memory.
